title: Sell Mineral Rights in Susquehanna County, PA
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Susquehanna County, PA
metaDescription: We buy dry-gas Marcellus mineral interests in Susquehanna County, explain your royalty statement honestly, and pay cash without dragging you into a bidding war.
heroLead: Susquehanna County was one of the very first places in Pennsylvania where a landman knocked on a farmhouse door and changed a family's finances overnight. Fifteen years later, a lot of those same families still don't fully trust the check that shows up.
intro: Long before Washington County or Greene County saw a Marcellus rig, Susquehanna County was already leased up. Cabot Oil & Gas, now Coterra, built one of the largest and most productive positions in the entire play here, and the county's dry-gas wells are still some of the most efficient producers in the Commonwealth. Montrose is the county seat, and the recorder of deeds office there has spent the better part of two decades processing lease assignments, division orders, and probate filings tied to gas.

That early start cuts both ways for the families who own minerals here now. On one hand, these are some of the longest-producing, best-understood wells in the Marcellus. On the other, a lot of the original leases were signed in 2008 and 2009, before landowners in this part of the state had much leverage or much legal advice, and those older lease terms are exactly the ones causing the most grief on today's royalty statements.

sections.heading: Dry Gas, Long Laterals, and Decades of Production History
paragraphs: Susquehanna County sits in the dry-gas core of the Marcellus, meaning the gas here is almost pure methane with little of the natural gas liquids you'd find further south and west. Operators compensate with scale: some of the longest laterals and largest pad developments in the state have been drilled here, and a single unit can span multiple family tracts. If you own a fractional interest in a Susquehanna County unit, it may be tied to a well that's been producing steadily for well over a decade, which gives us a strong production history to value your interest against rather than guessing at what a brand-new well might do.

That long track record is actually an advantage when you're deciding whether to sell. We can look at years of actual volumes instead of a projection, and that makes for a fairer, better-grounded offer.

sections.heading: Why So Many Early Leases Left Owners Exposed
paragraphs: A lot of the original Susquehanna County leases were signed at a pace that outran the legal advice available at the time. Post-production cost deduction language, in particular, was often boilerplate that favored the operator, and after the Kilmer v. Elexco ruling gave that language real teeth, owners here started seeing gathering, compression, and marketing fees carved out of their royalty before the one-eighth minimum required under Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act was ever calculated. We've reviewed statements from Susquehanna County families where the net check came in at little more than half the gross value of the gas.

It's not fraud, it's contract language most people signed without a landman or attorney explaining what it would mean fifteen years down the road. We don't judge anyone for that. We ask the same questions our own family had to learn to ask.

sections.heading: Act 13 Impact Fees in a County Built on Gas Revenue
paragraphs: Susquehanna County has depended on Act 13 impact fee distributions since the law passed in 2012, using the money for roads, emergency services, and local infrastructure that a rural county budget couldn't otherwise carry. That fee is paid by the well operator to the county and its municipalities, though, not to you as a mineral owner, and it has nothing to do with what shows up on your own royalty statement. Understanding that separation matters here more than almost anywhere else in the state, because Susquehanna County residents hear about impact fee money constantly and it's easy to conflate it with personal royalty income.

sections.heading: What Selling Looks Like for a Susquehanna County Owner
paragraphs: Because so many wells here have a long production history, we can often put together an offer faster than in newer counties. We pull your deed, confirm your interest against the unit and any pooling order on file, review recent statements if you have them, and give you a number based on real production, not a guess. Some owners sell a full interest, others carve out and sell a term interest while keeping the rest in the family. We close through a title company and record everything properly at the courthouse in Montrose.

faqs.question: Is Susquehanna County still an active drilling area?
faqs.answer: Yes, though the pace has slowed from the peak years. Existing wells continue producing, and infill development and refracturing still happen on established pads, which keeps many older units active.

faqs.question: My original lease was signed in 2008. Does it still apply?
faqs.answer: Most Marcellus leases from that era include a habendum clause that keeps the lease in force as long as the well is held by production, so yes, it likely still governs your interest even today.

faqs.question: Why is my royalty check so much smaller than I expected from the gross gas value?
faqs.answer: Post-production cost deductions, gathering, compression, dehydration, and marketing fees, are the most common reason. Pennsylvania's minimum royalty law guarantees one-eighth of the gross before most of those deductions, but many older leases allow deductions after that calculation.

faqs.question: Does the county impact fee affect my royalty payment?
faqs.answer: No. Act 13 impact fees go to county and municipal government from the well operator directly and have no bearing on the royalty calculation in your lease or division order.

faqs.question: Can you buy an interest I inherited that was never formally transferred?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, though we'll need to help you clear title through probate or an affidavit of heirship first. We can walk you through exactly what the recorder of deeds office in Montrose will require.
